--- title: "Fitting the Mean Field Before Kriging" jupyter: python3 fig-dpi: 300 execute: cache: false --- Kriging predicts a field as a mean field plus a GP anomaly. Where floats are sparse the anomaly reverts to zero and the map falls back on the mean field, so a mean field fitted to preferentially sampled profiles carries their bias into the gaps. This report compares four fits of the mean field on the toy jet of [the toy report](simex.qmd), two global and two local in the style of Roemmich--Gilson and Kuusela--Stein, each followed by the same kriging step. ## Toy with a meander and a seasonal cycle The field is the Bickley-jet OHC with a standing meander, plus a seasonal cycle whose amplitude varies with both latitude and longitude: $$ Z(x,y,t) = \underbrace{-\tanh(y/L) + m\,\operatorname{sech}^2(y/L)\cos(k_m x) + a(x,y)\cos\!\big(2\pi(t-t_0)/365\big)}_{\mu(x,y,t)} \;+\; \eta(x,y,t), $$ $$ a(x,y) = 0.3\,\big\{1+\tfrac12\tanh(y/L)\big\}\big\{1+\tfrac12\sin(2\pi x/L_x)\big\}, $$ with $m = 0\.3$, $k_m = 4\pi/L_x$ (wavelength $565$ km), and $\eta$ the travelling-eddy part of the jet streamfunction. The meander is a stationary mode of the streamfunction, so the floats and the clouds both follow it. The seasonal term is thermal only. $\eta$ and the meander integrate to zero over the periodic channel, so the box mean is $\bar Z(t) = \int Z(\cdot,t)\,d\mathbb P = 0.3\cos\{2\pi(t-t_0)/365\}$ exactly. Sixty floats are deployed uniformly on day $0$. After a one-year spin-up, $4$ years of $10$-day profiles give $146$ snapshots and $8{,}760$ profiles per replicate. In the example replicate below, 74% of profiles are in the warm southern half, and within a latitude band they also favour warm eddies: the anomaly $\eta$ averages \+0\.038 at the profiles against $0$ over the box. ::: {#f3de91af .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_setup(ex)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Z in the warm and cold seasons with that snapshot's floats, and the box mean through the record.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=1205 height=414} ::: ::: ## Four mean fits **Global fits.** One regression over the whole box on the basis $h(y,t)$: a cubic in $u = y/250$ km, the annual harmonics, and the harmonics times $u$. The basis has no $x$ terms, so it cannot represent the meander or the zonal change in seasonal amplitude; it stands in for a mean field fitted on too coarse a scale. $\log\hat q_t(x,y)$ is the stacked cloud density from anchors $4$ cycles back (as in the toy report), relative to uniform and floored at $0.05$. **Local fits.** Following Ridgway et al. (2002), Roemmich and Gilson (2009) and Kuusela and Stein (2018), for each centre $s^* = (x^*,y^*)$ of a $45 \times 20$ grid ($\approx 25$ km spacing), the window $\mathcal W(s^*) = [x^*-\lambda, x^*+\lambda]\times[y^*-\lambda,y^*+\lambda]$ with $\lambda = 150$ km (periodic in $x$) is formed, and the profiles in it are fitted by least squares to $$ m_{s^*}(x,y,t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\Delta_x + \beta_2\Delta_y + \beta_3\Delta_x\Delta_y + \beta_4\Delta_x^2 + \beta_5\Delta_y^2 + \sum_{k=1}^{6}\big\{\gamma_k\sin(2\pi k t/365) + \delta_k\cos(2\pi k t/365)\big\} + \nu_1(t-t_D) + \nu_2(t-t_D)^2, $$ with $(\Delta_x,\Delta_y) = (x-x^*, y-y^*)$ and $t_D$ the middle of the record. The window mean is $\hat\mu(s^*,t) = \hat m_{s^*}(s^*,t)$, the intercept, harmonics and trend. Off the centres, $\hat\mu(\cdot,t)$ is the bilinear interpolant of the centre coefficients; this interpolation is our choice, not part of the RG/KS specification. A window with fewer than $100$ profiles would be widened by $25\%$ steps. In the example replicate every window already has at least 286 profiles (median 1250). The local $+\log\hat q$ fit adds $\gamma\log\hat q_t(x,y)$ to $m_{s^*}$ and keeps $\hat\gamma_{s^*}\log\hat q_t$ in $\hat\mu$, so its $\hat q$ coefficient varies by window. | fit | coefficients | intuition | |---|---|---| | global OLS | $\hat\beta = (H^\top H)^{-1}H^\top z$ | every profile is one vote, one mean shape for the box | | global GLS + $\log\hat q$ | $\hat\beta = (H^\top K^{-1}H)^{-1}H^\top K^{-1}z$, $\log\hat q$ a column of $H$ | correlated profiles share a vote; crowded water may be warmer | | local LS (RG/KS) | ordinary least squares in each window | each place gets its own mean and seasonal cycle | | local LS + $\log\hat q$ | as local LS, with $\log\hat q$ a column in each window | as above, and crowding may be warmer, by a different amount in each window | $K$ is the anomaly covariance at the profiles: block diagonal by year (years as i.i.d. replicates), anisotropic exponential in $(x,y,t)$ with a $10^{-3}$ relative nugget. Its parameters are *oracle* values, the $e$-folding scales of the true $\eta$ ($\ell_x = 95$ km, $\ell_y = 210$ km, $\ell_t = 7$ d), so that only the mean-field step differs between fits. The local fits are ordinary least squares, as in RG/KS; $K$ enters them only through kriging. ::: {#3af3ed70 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_fits(ex)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Example replicate. Left: zonal mean of each fitted mean field against the zonal mean of the true mean field on one cold-season day (the zonal mean hides the meander). Middle: latitude distribution of all profiles (dashed: uniform). Right: box mean of each fitted mean field alone, against the truth.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=1419 height=418} ::: ::: Global OLS lets the crowded south and its warm eddies dominate, so its mean field runs warm. The local fit follows the meander and the zonal change in the seasonal amplitude, which lowers the root-mean-square error of the mean field over the box and the target days in this replicate from 0\.173 to 0\.102. Its box mean is nevertheless almost as warm as the global OLS mean (right panel). Least squares within a window is still one vote per profile, so each window is pulled toward the warm water its floats crowd into. The $\log\hat q$ column lets a fit attribute the extra warmth of crowded water to the crowding itself. Globally, $\hat\gamma = 0\.21$ here, and it also shifts the latitude coefficients, because $\hat q$ itself varies with latitude. $\hat\gamma$ is therefore part of a better prediction, not an interpretable effect. Within a $300$ km window $\log\hat q$ varies less and is close to collinear with the quadratic terms. The window coefficients $\hat\gamma_{s^*}$ are then noisy, and the local $+\log\hat q$ mean field is rougher than the local one (root-mean-square error 0\.151) but less biased in its box mean. ::: {#e8faf410 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_q_term(ex)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: expected float density q-hat on one day. Right: the true anomaly eta, with the contour where q-hat is twice uniform. Floats are expected where eta is warm.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=1291 height=407} ::: ::: ## Three estimators of the box mean **Kriging.** Each fitted mean field is followed by simple kriging of the residuals, $$ \hat Z_{\mathrm{K}}(t^*) \;=\; \int \hat\mu(\cdot,t^*)\,d\mathbb P \;+\; \sum_i w_i\,\big\{Z_i - \hat\mu(x_i)\big\}, $$ with block-kriging weights $w_i$ from all profiles within $\pm 30$ d of $t^*$. The weights depend only on the profile positions and $K$, so they are the same for the four fits; only the residuals differ. **Cross-fit DR, leave one float out.** For each float $f$, the map $\hat m^{(-f)}$ is the mean fit plus kriging computed without any of float $f$'s profiles; for the local fits every window is refit. In the two $\log\hat q$ fits, the covariate comes from the other floats' clouds only. The pooled $\hat q$ at a time after $t^*$ is anchored partly on float $f$'s own positions near $t^*$, so using it would let float $f$'s realized position into the map that float $f$ checks. With $q_f$ the cloud density of float $f$ (expected profiles per km$^2$), $q = \sum_f q_f$ the stacked density, and $|\mathcal X|$ the box area, $$ \hat Z_{\mathrm{DR}}(t^*) \;=\; \int \sum_{f}\frac{q_f}{q}\,\hat m^{(-f)}\,d\mathbb P \;+\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal X|}\sum_{f}\sum_{i\in f}\frac{Z_i - \hat m^{(-f)}(x_i)}{q(x_i)}\,\mathbf 1_{C}(x_i), $$ where $C = \{q\,|\mathcal X|/n \ge 0.05\}$ is the covered set. Off $C$ the $n$ maps are averaged with equal weight and no correction is made. The map term is not the full-data map. Each float's own influence on the map is removed in proportion to where that float was expected to be, which is what keeps a float from checking a map it helped build. Floats move independently given the flow. Conditional on the other floats, Campbell's theorem gives $\mathbb E\sum_{i\in f} g(x_i) = \int g\,q_f\,d\mu$, so if the clouds' density were exact, $$ \mathbb E\big[\hat Z_{\mathrm{DR}}(t^*)\big] - \bar Z(t^*) \;=\; -\int_{C^c}\Big(Z - \tfrac1n\textstyle\sum_f \mathbb E\,\hat m^{(-f)}\Big)\,d\mathbb P . $$ This is an exact identity, with a positivity remainder on the uncovered set only. With estimated densities $\hat q_f$ the bias picks up the product term $\sum_f\int (Z-\hat m^{(-f)})(q_f-\hat q_f)/\hat q\,d\mathbb P$. Under the correct cloud model, that error comes only from Monte Carlo and kernel smoothing in $\hat q_f$ ($200$ particles per cloud, $10$ km bandwidth) and from binning to the $5$ km grid. On average $C$ covers 99\.7% of the box. The DR step is applied to all four mean fits. Estimates are taken at every third snapshot of each of 30 replicates. The $60$ leave-one-out kriging maps share one cross-covariance per target. Each needs only the solve $K_{-f}^{-1}\,(Z-\hat\mu^{(-f)})$, so leave-one-float-out costs little more than a single map. ## One day, map by map The figures below follow the example replicate through one cold-season day (day 610) under the correct cloud model. All maps share the colour scale of $Z$, and all errors share one diverging scale. The box mean of each map is in its title. A single day shows how each estimator builds its answer, not how well it does on average; that is the next section. **Mean field.** Each fit's $\hat\mu(\cdot, t^*)$ next to the true $\mu$. The global fits vary only with latitude, as their basis allows, apart from the $\hat q$ pattern that the GLS $+\log\hat q$ fit adds. The local fits follow the meander. The local $+\log\hat q$ fit adds its window-by-window $\hat q$ term on top. ::: {#9fbf5a16 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_mean_maps(st)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Top: the true mean field and the four fitted mean fields on one day. Bottom: their errors, mapped and as a zonal mean by latitude.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=1676 height=651} ::: ::: **Mean field + kriging.** Kriging adds the anomaly near the floats. Where floats are dense the four maps agree and follow the eddies. In the gaps they fall back to their own mean field, so the mean-field errors above survive there. ::: {#aa9ee146 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_krige_maps(st)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Top: the true field with that day's floats, and the kriging map built on each mean field. Bottom: map errors, mapped and as a zonal mean by latitude.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=1676 height=651} ::: ::: **Cross-fit DR.** Top row: the map term, the mixture $\sum_f (q_f/q)\,\hat m^{(-f)}$ of the $60$ leave-one-float-out maps. Each float's own map is used where that float was expected to be, so the mixture is close to the kriging map but never lets a float check itself. Bottom row: each float's check $Z_i - \hat m^{(-f)}(x_i)$, coloured by the residual and sized by its weight $1/q$, over the faint error of the mixed map. Isolated floats far from the crowd get the largest weights: the northern floats are 27% of the floats on this day but carry 48% of the weight. The weighted sum of the checks is the correction added to the map term. ::: {#524960f0 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_dr_maps(st)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Top: weight of each float's check, and the mixed leave-one-out map for each mean fit. Bottom: map error by latitude, and each float's residual against its own leave-one-out map (size: weight).](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=1706 height=651} ::: ::: ::: {#170e364d .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_day_summary(st)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Box-mean estimate of every estimator on this day.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=990 height=495} ::: ::: ## Results under the correct cloud model ::: {#ce980165 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_errors(df)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Error of the box-mean estimate over 30 replicates and about 49 target days each, correct cloud model.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=988 height=649} ::: ::: ::: {#a72cbc9c .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} HTML(fmt(mf.summary(dc))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}

Adding $\log\hat q$ cuts the bias to \+0\.007 (global GLS) and \+0\.014 (local). For comparison, the simple mean of a snapshot's profiles is biased by \+0\.448. - **After kriging.** Kriging repairs the mean field where floats are dense. The biases become \+0\.021 (global OLS), \+0\.018 (local), \+0\.008 (global GLS + $\log\hat q$) and \-0\.0004 (local + $\log\hat q$). The last is within 1 Monte Carlo standard error of zero; with the correct cloud model, the local fit with the $\hat q$ covariate leaves no bias that kriging cannot remove. - **Cross-fit DR.** On the two maps without $\hat q$, DR is unbiased within Monte Carlo error: \-0\.0004 (global OLS map) and \-0\.0003 (local map). On the two $\log\hat q$ maps it is \+0\.0025 and \+0\.0032, which are small but 3 and 4 standard errors from zero. A likely cause, not yet tested, is that the covariate and the weights are built from the same cloud particles. The Monte Carlo error in $\hat q$ then enters both $\hat m^{(-f)}$ and $1/\hat q$, so the product term $\int (Z-\hat m)(q-\hat q)/\hat q\,d\mathbb P$ is no longer a product of independent errors. Building the covariate from independent particle draws would test this. - **Variance.** The local map gives the least variable DR estimate (sd 0\.028, against 0\.032 on the global OLS map), because its residuals are smaller. The local $+\log\hat q$ kriging map is still less variable than any DR estimate (sd 0\.016, RMSE 0\.016), so under the correct cloud model it has the lowest per-day RMSE. ``` ::: ::: With a wrong cloud model, DR is no longer unbiased. Its bias is then the product term: the map's residuals times the error in $\hat q$. The quality of the map starts to matter. - **Drift omitted, or noise too large.** The clouds no longer concentrate where floats actually gather, so the weights are too flat and the correction is too small. The local $+\log\hat q$ map gives the smallest DR bias in both cases (\+0\.0051 and \+0\.0056), at most half that of the other three maps (\+0\.0137 and \+0\.0144 on the global OLS map). - **Eddies displaced.** $\hat q$ is high in the wrong places, so the covariate carries little information (the global $\hat\gamma$ falls to 0\.053), and the four DR estimators end up similar (\+0\.0129 to \+0\.0162). That is still below the kriging maps' bias. - **Noise too small.** This is the dangerous direction. Clouds that are too tight give floats landing in their thin tails very large weights, so DR over-corrects. On the maps without $\hat q$ the bias becomes \-0\.0245 (global OLS) and \-0\.0208 (local), larger in size than the uncorrected kriging bias and of the opposite sign. On the $\log\hat q$ maps, whose residuals are small, it is \-0\.0065 (global) and \+0\.0057 (local). Coverage also drops to 95% on average. Across all five cloud models, the largest absolute DR bias is 0\.0139 on the local $+\log\hat q$ map, against 0\.0208 on the local map, 0\.0245 on the global OLS map, and 0\.0182 for the local $+\log\hat q$ kriging map alone. A good map limits how much a wrong $\hat q$ can hurt. And since too little cloud noise costs more than too much, the noise should be calibrated, or erred on the wide side. **Not included here.** The covariance is oracle. An Argo-only version would estimate $K$ from the profiles, which preferential sampling also biases. That affects only the maps, not the validity argument for the DR step. The window half-width $\lambda$ was fixed at $150$ km and not tuned.
